how was Hercules Mulligan an american spy?





Hercules Mulligan’s spying was basically human intelligence hidden inside his day job. He was a successful tailor in British-occupied New York City, and many of his customers were wealthy and high-ranking British officers. That gave him extraordinary access to people who knew British military plans. 

CIA
+1
After the Americans lost New York in 1776, Alexander Hamilton—then serving on George Washington’s staff—recommended Mulligan when Washington needed someone who could operate inside the occupied city. Mulligan stayed in New York and continued acting like an ordinary businessman friendly with British officers. 

CIA

His method was surprisingly simple. While fitting officers for uniforms, he would chat with them, flatter them, and casually ask questions. Even mundane tailoring information could reveal military plans. For example, if several officers suddenly needed repaired uniforms returned by the same date, Mulligan could infer that their unit was preparing to move. British officers also sometimes simply talked too much around a civilian tailor they did not regard as a threat. 

CIA
+1

The crucial second half of the operation was Cato, an enslaved Black man working with Mulligan. Cato carried intelligence out of British-controlled New York to Washington's headquarters, at enormous personal risk; he was reportedly captured and beaten on one mission. So the operation is better thought of as Mulligan + Cato, rather than Mulligan doing everything himself. 

CIA

The most famous example supposedly happened when a British officer urgently came to Mulligan for a coat. Mulligan asked why he needed it so quickly, and the officer revealed that he was about to take part in an operation to capture George Washington. Mulligan sent Cato with the warning, allowing Washington to avoid the ambush. A second warning came in 1781, when Mulligan’s brother Hugh learned that British troops were preparing to intercept Washington on his way to Rhode Island; again the information reached Washington and he changed his route. 

CIA
+1

One important distinction: Mulligan was not actually a member of the famous Culper Spy Ring. Washington operated several intelligence networks. The Culper Ring was one of them; Mulligan was a separate agent working inside New York. Mount Vernon specifically lists him among Washington’s other agents outside the Culper organization. 

George Washington's Mount Vernon

So the Hamilton line—

“A tailor spyin’ on the British government”
—is basically accurate. His tailor shop was an extremely good intelligence-gathering post because British officers voluntarily walked in, stood around for fittings, and talked to him about exactly the information Washington wanted.
